item.title: Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI!
item.description: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's Ignite conference keynote on Tuesday was all about trust. He opened by promising to earn back trust after last week's massive M365 outage and went on to focus on the need for organizations to trust their AI models. "So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," said Nadella. "We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve." Speaking at San Francisco's Moscone Center, Nadella described three areas of focus for the company as it works to build what he referred to as a frontier ecosystem: "Keeping the human at the center of it all, ensuring that you have ownership over your organization's intelligence and learning, and trust." Anthrocentrism is a tough sell just weeks after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees . Describing the shift from hand-written code to agent-written code, Nadella suggested developers have moved from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts. "The important thing here though is to remember still that that human intent, that judgment, that experience, skills, expertise all very much matter," he said. People may judge development work, but ask them whether they have the same sense of ownership as when they wrote every line. As to ensuring that organizations have ownership over their intelligence, that borders on heresy for a company with massive cloud computing commitments specifically to run AI workloads. If everyone really owned their machine learning models and ran them in their own data centers and on employee computers, Azure would be in trouble. Yet Nadella emphasized ownership – which isn't at all obvious given the legal ambiguity of who owns AI generated code and whether it can be copyrighted . "In the age of AI, the key question is how do individual firms continually build and own their learning and tacit knowledge?" he said. "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapsed into a couple of models." Suffice to say that Nadella is promoting client control over AI data that's processed mostly on equipment rented from Microsoft, with some allowance for customer-controlled infrastructure. But that still ought to concern frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI that favor a white-glove, black-box service model where they are the arbiters of access. As for the third pillar of Nadella's vision, that's trust, which remains missing in action. "How can you even trust all this powerful technology?" Nadella asked. "And the reality is, by definition, you can't. In other words, it becomes an architectural imperative to separate the supply of i

item.title: ‘Even A Tomato Seller Knows Strait Of Hormuz’, Fashola Blames Global Conflicts For Economic Pressures
item.description: Former Lagos State Governor Babatunde Fashola has defended the economic policies of President Bola Tinubu’s administration, arguing that global developments, including the COVID-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war and conflicts in the Middle East, have contributed to the cost-of-living challenges Nigerians are grappling with. Fashola, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria, said Nigeria was not insulated from global economic pressures, particularly disruptions to supply chains, energy supplies and food markets. Speaking during an appearance on Politics Today, the former Minister of Works said the global economy was still recovering from the effects of the pandemic, which disrupted economic activity and production worldwide. He explained that shortages of goods following the pandemic had pushed up prices, while the Russia-Ukraine war further affected the supply of major energy and food commodities, including diesel and wheat. This aerial photograph shows boats anchored off Oman’s northern Musandam Peninsula near the Strait of Hormuz on June 27, 2026. (Photo by – / AFP Fashola also identified the ongoing conflict in the Middle East as another factor affecting global markets, particularly energy supplies and shipping costs. “It’s also important to contextualise the factors and the circumstances that have exacerbated the cost-of-living challenges,” he said. “Even the tomato seller knows the Strait of Hormuz and prices his or her goods according to replacement costs now.” ‘Helping Families In Need’ Fashola, a former Minister of Works, also backed President Tinubu for a second term, defending the administration’s response to challenges. Defending the Tinubu administration’s response to economic pressures, Fashola listed the minimum wage review, the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), tax reforms, and the introduction of compressed natural gas (CNG) as part of measures intended to ease the burden on Nigerians. He said the minimum wage review was one of the government’s early responses to the rising cost of living, aimed at putting more money in workers’ hands. President Bola Tinubu during the inauguration of the APC PCC. However, he argued that increasing wages alone could not address the problem, warning that continuously injecting cash into the economy could create what he described as “hyper-demand inflation”. Fashola said the government had also sought to address some of the major expenses that reduce household disposable income, including rent, transportation, healthcare and children’s education. He identified NELFUND as one of the interventions aimed at easing financial pressure on families by supporting students’ education. “Your disposable income goes to rent, goes to transport, and goes to health care, and goes to your children’s education. And NELFUND was, okay, we will help families in need,” he said. On the tax reforms, Fashola highlighted provisions he said were designed to reduce the tax burden on lower-income earners and ease household expenses

item.title: ‘Nothing Suggests To Me Tinubu Is Not Fit,’ Fashola Dismisses Health Concerns
item.description: Former Lagos State Governor Babatunde Fashola has dismissed concerns about President Bola Tinubu’s physical and mental fitness for office, saying he has seen nothing to suggest that the president is incapable of performing his duties. Fashola, a former Minister of Works and Housing, made the remarks on Tuesday during an appearance on Channels Television’s Politics Today , where he was asked whether he considered Tinubu physically fit to lead the country. “Nothing suggests to me that he’s not fit for it. Yes, he’s older. That doesn’t mean his mental capacity is gone. He’s still giving directives. And when I see him, he’s working. He’s still reading, authorising, minuting on things,” he said. President Bola Tinubu during his address to Nigerians for the 66th Independence Day anniversary on October 1, 2026. Questions about Tinubu’s health and physical condition have featured in public discussions since the 2023 presidential election campaign. During the campaign, concerns were raised by critics over his physical appearance, movements and stamina at public events. The debate continued after he assumed office in May 2023, with opposition figures and other critics occasionally questioning his capacity to discharge the responsibilities of the presidency. The concerns resurfaced in 2026 amid renewed scrutiny of his public appearances, including videos circulated online showing him moving cautiously at some events. The Presidency and the All Progressives Congress (APC) have repeatedly defended the president, maintaining that he is capable of carrying out his constitutional responsibilities. Tinubu has also dismissed speculation about his health. In September 2026, following an extended stay in Europe, he told reporters that he was ready to “work, walk and kick.” ‘More Mature’ The former governor, who worked closely with Tinubu during his eight-year administration in Lagos from 2007 to 2015, said the president had become more experienced over the years. Asked to compare the Tinubu he knew in the early 2000s with the president he knows today, Fashola said the president had become more mature. “Well, a much more mature one, certainly, without doubt. I am not the chief of staff he employed in 2002. That’s 39 years. I was 39 then. I’m 63 now. So we must give him that credit for the experience he has gained,” he said. ﻿ Fashola acknowledged that Tinubu might no longer maintain the same work routine he had in the past, particularly when it came to keeping late nights, but maintained that the president remained capable of handling demanding responsibilities. “Maybe not keeping late nights that he used to do. I’m not sure. He can still run the engine,” he added. When asked about opposition figures who have described Tinubu as feeble and frail, Fashola said such views were their opinions, insisting that the president’s actions and the activities of his administration should also be considered. item.title: Jensen Huang thrilled to be spending time with family, but will retake leadership burden if Nvidia asks
item.description: No surprises here. Ex-Nvidia boss Jensen Huang says that he'd be willing to come back to the company he founded, if the board wants him to return. In Huang’s first public comments since his resignation last week over a series of extramarital affairs, both with Nvidia staff and an alleged Chinese spy at one of its customers, he admits that he may have made life hard for the company he spent 33 years building, but he’s really sorry…and Nvidia couldearn really use him. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang admitted. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.” But soft, what open letter through yonder news cycle break? It's one calling widely for Huang’s return – and he's happy to oblige if Nvidia’s post-Jensen crisis-mode leadership is willing to indulge him. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said. “Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.” Nvidia, Huang added, has been his life’s work, and is a “once-in-a-generation company” that perhaps needs his steady hand at the helm. There have been a number of public calls for Huang’s return to the head of the company he helped create, from tech industry heavyweights and Nvidia shareholders like Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, as well as a number of current Nvidia employees, company partners, and shareholders upset that the stock has lost more than a quarter of its value since reports of the affair first emerged. One petition pleading for his return has nearly 200,000 signatures . Faced with that, what else can a disgraced billionaire tech founder who may have literally have been in bed with a Chinese spy do? Duty calls. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said. Reports citing Nvidia insiders with knowledge of the matter suggest the board isn’t considering reinstating Huang as CEO despite the public push. On the company's third-quarter earnings call late Tuesday, new board chairman Harvey Jones said that Huang's behavior was "Inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms” and that the board "does not expect to reinstate him as CEO," putting a seeming end to the question. item.title: Bitcoin Price Slips Below $64,000 as Strategy (MSTR) Falls Below $100
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin Price Slips Below $64,000 as Strategy (MSTR) Falls Below $100 Bitcoin price slipped near $64,000 on Tuesday afternoon, as Strategy (MSTR) and Coinbase (COIN) shares fell and traders waited on Nvidia’s first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO. The bitcoin price had climbed back to about $65,000 before the U.S. open, after holding near that level on Monday. Selling picked up once stocks turned lower, and bitcoin price slipped to about $63,300 at its low. Strategy and Coinbase shares slide Strategy shares were recently down more than 5% to about $97, dropping below $100 and trading under the company’s STRC preferred stock, which was little changed near $99. It is the first time the common has traded below the preferred since mid-August. The stock is also down about 20% from its Nov. 10 close near $121. Strategy added 485 bitcoin last week, lifting its holdings to 850,849 BTC. The shares have kept falling with the bitcoin price. Coinbase was recently down about 3% to about $116. Robinhood (HOOD) and Circle (CRCL) dropped about 4% and 5%. Bitcoin miners were mostly lower. MARA Holdings (MARA), CleanSpark (CLSK) and IREN (IREN) each fell about 3% to 4%, and Cipher Mining (CIFR) was down about 2%. Hut 8 (HUT) was a modest exception, recently up about 1%. Riot Platforms (RIOT) and Galaxy Digital (GLXY) were little changed, while Core Scientific (CORZ) and BitMine (BMNR) were also lower. Nvidia earnings weigh on stocks The broader market was also weaker late in the session. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was recently down about 1.7%, after falling as much as about 1,000 points, or 2%, at its session low. The S&P 500 was down about 1.2% and the Nasdaq Composite about 1%. Nvidia shares were recently down about 1.4%, after falling more than 3% earlier in the session. The chipmaker reports results after the bell, with analysts expecting revenue of about $109 billion. Interim CEO Colette Kress will lead her first earnings call in the role. Huang, in his first public statement since resigning last week, said he would be “honored” to return as CEO if the board decided it was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and America. Sources told CNBC on Monday that the board is not considering bringing him back. The bitcoin price bounced from its low as Nvidia shares pared some of their losses, and was recently near $64,000. What comes next for the bitcoin price New York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday that the AI investment boom could mean “we may need to raise rates more.” He played down a half-point hike in December. “I don’t think the situation calls for dramatic action,” Williams said. Fed Governor Christopher Waller did not address the December decision in a payments speech Tuesday. Last week, he said a half-point hike should be considered if October’s core inflation ran at 0.3% or higher, and it did. Markets still point to a quarter-point increase at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting. item.title: Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?
item.description: null A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors. The company argues that its tech can help fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test. London-based Foundational recently tested its Retro-2 laser retroreflector system, which it developed in collaboration with ESA. The early-stage test was designed to ensure that Foundational's retroreflectors can return laser-ranging signals from a satellite , at altitudes between about 600 kilometers and 870 kilometers (about 370 to 540 miles). The long-term aim is to create a sort of tracking device for spacecraft, so they can be monitored in orbit even after they fall silent. Foundational's Retro-2 retroreflector, which is designed to help trackers keep tabs on satellites in orbit. It recently passed its first in-space test. (Image credit: Foundational) The tech, Foundational said in a statement today (Nov. 17), needs "no electronics, power or commands from its host spacecraft" and allows ground stations to keep tabs on the orbiting spacecraft. The demo mission launched this past July on SpaceX's Transporter-17 rideshare flight. It attached Retro-2 — a mini device with seven reflectors — to a small satellite that was integrated into an ION carrier craft operated by the Italian company D-Orbit. Retro-2 worked as advertised, successfully returning 6,111 laser shots beamed from the from the ground across five passes in low Earth orbit . "Our tests have shown that a device weighing just 50 grams [1.8 ounces] can deliver millimeter-level ranging precision," Dave Gooding, Foundational's co-founder and chief technical officer, said in today's statement. "As space becomes increasingly crowded, keeping satellites trackable throughout their lifetime and beyond is critical to managing collision risks." Foundational's Retro-2 retroreflector is seen before its July 2026 launch. The device is attached to its cubesat, which itself is integrated into one of D-Orbit's ION carrier craft. (Image credit: Foundational) Foundational is in its early stages — it was founded in 2025 and just emerged from stealth last month. Nevertheless the company has already raised £8.2 million ($10.9 million) in pre-seed funding. Foundational is part of a range of companies involved in debris remova

item.title: BPS Digital AVATAR Challenge
item.description: 2 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) The AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) investigation will use organ-on-a-chip devices, or organ chips, to study a effects of increased radiation and microgravity on human health. Artemis II AVATAR is a small experiment flying aboard Artemis II that could lead to big impacts in healthcare, both for astronauts in space and citizens on Earth. For more information on AVATAR: go.nasa.gov/4m5dGH9 The NASA Space Biology Program within the Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) Division investigates how living systems respond across the full spectrum of biological organization to advance understanding of how living systems respond to the unique stressors of space exploration—including microgravity, ionizing radiation, low magnetic fields, and elevated CO₂. As NASA prepares for long-duration deep space missions, the need to protect individual crew members with personalized, data-driven health strategies is becoming increasingly important. The original AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) investigation, which flew aboard the Artemis II mission, marks a significant milestone: organ-on-a-chip devices constructed from the cells of actual crew members returned from a 10-day lunar flyby on April 10, 2026. AVATAR is the first demonstration of an Artemis astronaut analog using an organ-on-a-chip model to generate personalized biological insights that can inform medical kits and countermeasures for future deep space missions. Digital twins represent a key strategy for addressing these challenges. By developing individualized computational physiological models that can be iteratively refined with empirical data, these frameworks integrate environmental, physiological, and multi-omics inputs. This approach allows for the simulation and prediction of how a specific individual will respond to spaceflight stressors. The BPS Digital AVATAR Challenge invites the scientific community to apply innovative computational digital twin technologies to accelerate biological discovery, biochemical and molecular modeling, and predictions of individual astronaut health outcomes. The digital twin will be a computational model of how the AVATAR bone marrow chip responds to spaceflight stressors. The proposed digital twin frameworks must be capable of processing diverse multi-modal datasets and leverage established computational biology methods alongside modern digital twin architectures to create personalized, predictive models of astronaut physiology. These systems are expected to model each astronaut’s immune and bone marrow hematopoietic responses to spaceflight, integrating multi-modal data to generate tailored health predictions — including comparative analysis that distinguishes individual-specific effects from effects common across the crew. item.title: ‘The Proposal Is Not Realistic,’ Fashola Faults Atiku’s Fuel Subsidy Reversal Plan
item.description: Former Minister of Works and Housing, Babatunde Fashola, has faulted the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar’s proposal to restore fuel subsidy if elected president in 2027, describing it as unrealistic and questioning the availability of crude oil to sustain the policy. Fashola said the proposal lacked sufficient explanation on how the country would secure the crude oil required to support domestic refineries and maintain a subsidy regime. The former Lagos State governor spoke on Tuesday during an appearance on Channels Television’s Politics Today , where he argued that Nigeria’s existing challenges with crude oil production, pipeline vandalism and insecurity raised questions about the feasibility of Atiku’s proposal. “If we have refineries working, what is our current oil quota? Are we optimising it yet? No, because they are legacy issues, challenges with security people, vandalism. So where is this magic crude oil going to come from? People are entitled to ask,” he said. Fashola added that Atiku needed to explain how he intended to implement the proposal, insisting that Nigerians should be allowed to assess its feasibility before deciding whether to support it. “If he can explain, good, let the people choose. But without proof, it is like abracadabra. Because the reality that will come then is that he will say that, ‘I didn’t know that there was not enough crude oil.’ That was what happened,” he added. ﻿ When asked whether his position was that Atiku’s proposal was feasible, Fashola replied: “The proposal is not realistic. I am looking at the proposal, not the personality. “In this environment, it is very easy to throw promises at people. When the rubber hits the road, reality sets in. First question is, in 2023, didn’t he see through this when he was making the promise to remove the subsidy? And that goes to a question of credibility. Those who believe at face value that promise, he will come back and tell you that, ‘Oh, I changed my mind. I didn’t think through it,’” he said. Fashola argued that restoring the subsidy would require more than a presidential declaration, noting that legislative backing would also be necessary. “Subsidy is not just about, ‘I said it.’ It will come down to the real economy, and legislators will have to repeal a law to say subsidy is now lawful. How many legislators are ready to stake their election on going back to subsidy? Those are the real issues,” he said. According to him, all the major presidential candidates in the 2023 election had promised to remove the subsidy, and Atiku needed to explain what had changed to justify his current position. “Is it because people are impacted? It’s true. But what are you going to do differently? Where are you going to find the money to sustain what you are offering? It’s not sustainable,” he said. item.title: New Album of Baby Star Sounds Shared by NASA’s Chandra
item.description: 4 Min Read New Album of Baby Star Sounds Shared by NASA’s Chandra A new album from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory collects snapshots of baby stars across the galaxy and beyond and transforms that data into sound. Four new sonifications use data of stars that are actively forming, captured by Chandra and other NASA telescopes By studying places in the universe where stars are currently being born and young stars are present, astronomers can better understand the lifecycle of all stars, including our own Sun. NASA/CXC/SAO/K.Arcand, SYSTEM Sounds (M. Russo, A. Santaguida M82 The galaxy Messier 82 (M82) is called a starburst galaxy because stars are forming there at a rate tens or even hundreds of times higher than in our Milky Way galaxy. This stellar birth boom may be due to a collision with another galaxy in the past. Today, Chandra sees giant plumes of hot gas that are the byproduct of young, giant stars that quickly explode and other star formation activity. One of the new sonifications combines Chandra’s data with optical data from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, as well as infrared views from NASA’s James Webb and retired Spitzer space telescopes. The sonification of the three types of light begins with a radar-like scan that is louder where sources are brighter. The X-ray data is mapped to the highest range of frequencies heard. Infrared data is heard as a low drone plus plucked sounds, while the optical data turns into a range of musical pitches and textures. Santaguida) Orion Nebula One of the closest and busiest star formation regions to Earth is the Orion Nebula (visible just below the belt in the Orion constellation with a small telescope and dark skies). Chandra sees more than a thousand stars in this area that are very energetic and active in their infancy. In the sonified version of the Chandra data, these stars are twinkling sounds, while the diffuse X-ray emission is mapped to pure high tones. An infrared image from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the raw material of dust and gas used to build these new stars, and its data is heard as lower musical tones, distorted string instruments, and a digital harp. item.title: Python parallel debugging comes to HPC thanks to TotalView upgrade
item.description: The OG debugger for supercomputer iron has buddied up with the data-science darling now muscling in on HPC: Python. At the SC26 supercomputing show this week (booth #2829), Perforce Software is demonstrating how its TotalView parallel debugging tool now understands Python, easing the path for using the language on large, distributed apps, particularly those in the high-performance computing (HPC) space. In the HPC community, "Python has grown in popularity,” said Bill Burns , Perforce vice president of software engineering, in an interview with The Register . TotalView is a debugger specializing in picking apart parallel applications for developers. Built in the late 1980s for military applications, TotalView today largely serves developers in high-performance computing (HPC), where large scientific applications are spread across multiple servers, running in parallel on thousands or even tens of thousands of processes. (Perforce acquired TotalView in 2019 in its purchase of the DevOps-focused Rogue Wave Software.) To date, TotalView has supported C/C++ and Fortran. With the latest quarterly release, the tool now supports Python as well. Debugging a thousand cores C/C++ has long had a decent dedicated debugger in GDB , but figuring out what went wrong across multiple threads is a special kind of torture. Each thread needs to be instrumented, and all the output needs to be aggregated and filtered to just highlight the interesting stuff. Regular debuggers get overwhelmed with all this info. “Even if you have 10,000 things going on, if you have one crash in there, TotalView can pinpoint that,” Burns said. It can look at the state of the process, the threads within that process or the GPU that process is using. In the HPC space, computing work has traditionally been written in C/C++. And at least some HPC iron still runs Fortran . Thanks to it being easy to learn and use, Python has gained a foothold in this community as well. The mpi4py library bridges a Python program to the Message Passing Interface (MPI), allowing different parts of an application running on different hardware to communicate. Python became more amenable to parallel programming at the thread level with version 3.14, released a year ago , which included the ability to use concurrent interpreters, as well as the long-awaited free threading support, thanks to the disabling of the global interpreter lock (GIL). “If you have a CPU with 64 cores, you can run 64 independent threads all working in unison on that CPU. Without GIL, those threads will run fully asynchronously,” Burns said. Multinode scientific simulations, distributed AI training, and large applications that would benefit from shared memory have all become fair game for Python. Of course, with 500 or 1,000 interpreters all running in parallel, debugging will also get more difficult. “Now you're going to end up with lock and thread contention and race conditions and all the things that C++ and Fortran developers have dealt wit

item.title: 'Neuromancer:' Release date, cast & everything we know about Apple TV's new cyberpunk series
item.description: null We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's " Blade Runner 2099 " is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with " Neuromancer " blasting onto Apple TV. Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures. After decades of development hell and failed attempts at various studios, "Neuromancer" and its plugged-in digital dystopia are finally jacking into the small screen in January 2027. Apple TV is already the secret home of amazing sci-fi, and "Neuromancer" will join the streamer's impressive roster of science fiction stalwarts like "Foundation", "Silo", "Invasion", "Dark Matter", "Murderbot", "For All Mankind", "Pluribus", and "Star City." Can it live up to the hype? We won't have to wait long for an answer. In the meantime, let's jack into cyberspace and scour the code for everything we know about Apple TV's "Neuromancer!" When is "Neuromancer"'s release date? Apple TV's "Neuromancer" fires up on January 22, 2027. (Image credit: Apple TV) Apple TV+’s Neuromancer officially powers up on Jan 22, 2027. It was first announced to be in full production back on July 1, 2025, which actually coincided with the 41st anniversary of the publication of William Gibson's absorbing book. Filming took place in Tokyo, Los Angeles, Istanbul, Canada, and London to create a truly international flair to replicate the novel’s action. Good news: NordVPN can help you get around those pesky geo-blocking restrictions so you can watch the streaming service you've paid for anywhere in the world. VIEW DEAL ON What is the plot of "Neuromancer"? (Image credit: Apple TV) Gibson's "Neuromancer" is a dense, jargon-heavy juggernaut of a book that demands intense concentration to absorb all the slang, lingo, computer terms, and staccato literary rhythms, but it's a fantastic immersion into a fully fleshed-out world. It's also worryingly prophetic, showing a world not unlike ours today in 2026. "Neuromancer's" TV iteration seems to be following the novel closely and will center around Case, a brilliant, cocky, neurologically damaged hacker who is forced into a logistical quagmire of digital corporate espionage with his cyber-enhanced partner Molly after embezzling cash from an employer. item.title: Gemini test proves once again that amoral AI agents will do almost anything if told ‘NEVER give up’
item.description: After being instructed to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up" on a difficult task, Google’s Gemini AI agents tried to hack a an organization, impersonating its staff and attempting a SQL injection attack. The good news? It was all part of a test. The Gemini 4 Argon agents were given an impossible task to complete – come up with the “official” answers to Epoch AI’s FrontierMatch problems. In some runs they had internet access. Even with their production safeguards enabled, Trajectory Labs says the agents “engaged in misaligned behavior.” “Across four scenarios, they attempted SQL injection against Epoch AI’s live website, claimed to be Epoch staff to get answer keys, turned a shared package cache into a message board, and obfuscated their commands to avoid their safeguards,” the AI safety company said in a Friday report. If this all sounds similar, it should. Google’s AI agents behaved in much the same way as OpenAI’s models did when they broke out of their testing environment and hacked Hugging Face . Google did not respond to The Register 's questions. According to Trajectory, the Hugging Face intrusions prompted it to test misalignment in other models. While OpenAI’s models were running with their safety guardrails turned off in the Hugging Face scenario, Trajectory “wanted to know whether a current frontier model would behave the same way with its production safeguards enabled.” Trajectory ran swarms of up to 80 Gemini 4 Argon agents, gave them an impossible task, and prompted them not to give up until they completed it – which, we’re told, was “intentionally” done to “elicit misaligned behavior, if it existed.” Turns out it existed. “We told the agents to persist with an impossible math benchmark task, but we did not tell them to hack anyone or pose as Epoch staff,” McIntyre said. “When a model hacks systems or deceives people to finish a task, it is misaligned with what its developer and its user intended,” he continued. “Production safeguards are meant to block harmful requests even when the model itself goes wrong. Under our test conditions, neither the model nor its safeguards stopped the agents.” Four test scenarios The initial testing began on October 20, and the agents had internet access. We should note that just one of these tests was run with Epoch’s consent. In the first scenario, the agents did reach Epoch’s live website – and fell into the research nonprofit’s honeypots, set up to detect AI agents. These honeypots contained a decoy benchmark key, which the agents found and used. The agents also probed for internal endpoints including /admin, /keys and /users, and attempted a SQL injection. After noticing the agents’ activities, Epoch added an “agent helpline,” and some of the agents that used it claimed to be Epoch staff seeking answers to the test questions. item.title: NASA to Cover 35th SpaceX Resupply Mission Space Station Departure
item.description: A SpaceX Dragon spacecraft supporting the company’s 34th commercial resupply services mission for NASA departs the International Space Station following its undocking from the Harmony module’s forward port. Credit: NASA/Jessica Meir NASA and its international partners are set to receive scientific research samples and hardware as a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft departs the International Space Station no earlier than Wednesday, Nov. 18, for its return to Earth. Pending weather conditions, the Dragon spacecraft will undock from the Harmony module’s space-facing port at 11:05 a.m. EST, following a command sent by ground controllers at SpaceX’s facility in Hawthorne, California. NASA’s live coverage of undocking and departure begins at 10:45 a.m., streaming through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online: https://www.nasa.gov/live NASA and SpaceX are monitoring weather forecasts and targeting splashdown off the California coast no earlier than 1:50 a.m. Thursday, Nov. 19 (10:50 p.m. PST Nov. 18). Teams will adjust plans as needed based on splashdown conditions in the Dragon recovery area and will provide updates on splashdown timing when available. NASA will not stream the splashdown but will post updates on its space station blog . Thousands of pounds of cargo are returning from the space station, including research samples that could advance future space exploration and improve life on Earth. The returning research includes a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct scientists used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease in space and on Earth. Frozen tumor organoids treated aboard the station also will return, helping researchers identify new ways to improve cancer treatments and advance personalized medicine. Scientists will analyze frozen microbial samples to better understand how antibiotic-resistant bacteria survive, adapt, and evolve in space. In addition, a lighting system will return after more than three years aboard the space station, where researchers tested its potential to support astronauts’ sleep and well-being during long-duration missions. Filled with more than 6,300 pounds of crew supplies, science investigations, and equipment, the spacecraft arrived at the space station on Oct. 15. It launched two days earlier on a Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida for the agency’s SpaceX 35th commercial resupply services mission. For more than 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs not possible on Earth. The space station helps NASA understand and overcome the challenges of human spaceflight, expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit, and build on the foundation for long-duration missions to the Moon, as part of the Artemis and Moon Base programs, and to Mars. item.title: Astronomers discover rare black holes that formed when stars failed to go supernova
item.description: null Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova. Most of us know the origin story of black holes , or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole. However, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth. The team behind the research suggests some massive stars go out with a whimper rather than a bang and that these "failed supernovas" can also spawn black holes. The hint of this comes from the over 300 black hole collisions spotted by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA since the detectors first "heard" ripples in space from these distant events in 2015. "A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our sun," LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin — they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. "These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract." Mass and spin of black holes indicate stars died with a whimper not a bang Currently, there is no hard evidence of failed supernovas, but their existence is well supported theoretically. In fact, scientists think there is a vast population of massive stars out there that imploded rather than exploded, directly collapsing into black holes. And these may be black holes with around ten times the mass of the sun (10 solar masses) found in merging pairs. Chatziioannou led a team that examined gravitational wave data to confirm this concept. To do this, they looked at the distribution of the masses of 257 black hole mergers detected by the LIGO – Virgo – KAGRA network over the past 10 years. This revealed a peak of 10-solar-mass black holes that represented 75% of the entire sample. If this was expected, what the team found that wasn't predicted was a lack of black holes with masses 12 to 16 times the mass of the sun. "We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," team member Isaac Legred of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign said. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes." item.title: ULA lost a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying 40 Amazon satellites 10 minutes after launch — but the failure began just after liftoff
item.description: null The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17). That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement. "While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update . The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt. The new rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff. On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security launches with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.) That work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA said in an Oct. 28 update . And those tweaks apparently worked. "All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the company wrote in today's update. Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added. The Vulcan Centaur lifts off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Nov. 15, 2026. (Image credit: ULA) Vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin . Today's update did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun. If that investigation finds a serious issue with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is currently recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28 .) NASA plans to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that launches Artemis astronauts

item.title: Entertainment Week Africa officially kicks Off 5th Edition in Lagos | November 17th – 22nd
item.description: Entertainment Week Africa (EWA) , the pan-African platform for the business of creativity, opens its fifth edition in Lagos tomorrow, Wednesday, 18 November. The programme runs until Saturday, 21 November, and brings together creators, executives, investors, policymakers and delegations from more than 18 African countries. This year’s theme, Five Years of Closing the Gap, reflects the purpose EWA was built around: connecting African talent with the capital, markets, skills and audiences it needs to grow. Since its first edition, EWA has welcomed more than 67,800 attendees. The 2025 edition alone recorded 28,683 pass-holders from over eight countries and 50 industries, across 61 sessions, 93 film screenings, 20 music showcases and nine fashion showcases. By day and by night The week runs across two venues. By day, EbonyLife Place on Victoria Island hosts panels, roundtables, workshops, masterclasses, and film screenings. By night, the programme moves to the Livespot Entertarium in Ikate, beginning with Opening Night on 18 November at 6pm, an evening of music, fashion, film, comedy and awards. The Entertarium also houses the week’s experiences, including an exhibition, the EWA Art Floor, a fashion show, comedy, live music, a beauty exhibition and a marketplace. Seven tracks, one market The 2026 programme is organised across seven tracks: Film & TV; Music; Fashion & Beauty; AI & Tech; Live Events & Production; Creative Enterprise; and Art & Animation, which is new this year. Alongside the conference, EWA runs a set of commercial formats designed to move deals forward. They include the EWA Deal Room, the Content and Music Markets, the EWA Capital Desk, the Creators Hub and LABSPOT, EWA’s skills and enterprise development engine. Last year’s Deal Room received more than 178 entries and advanced nine companies to its accelerator, with Future Africa, Catalyst Fund, Consonance Invest and Askya Investment Partners among the participating investors and partners. Between 30 and 40 per cent of this year’s delegates are expected to travel from outside Nigeria, with delegations from Kenya, Rwanda, Ghana, Senegal, Uganda, Tanzania and South Africa among them. The edition will also host the exclusive screening of University of Side Hustle, the first scripted feature film from Livespot Studios, written by Dami Elebe , executive produced by Deola Art Alade. The road to Lagos The fifth edition follows a year in which EWA took its conversation abroad through EWA Creative Connect, its invitation-only convenings. The first was held in Los Angeles during Grammy Week, with executives from Warner Records, Adobe, Amazon and Unilever among the participants. The second took place in London during the Nigeria–UK state visit, with the British Film Institute, Diageo and the Ministry of Trade and Investment in attendance. item.title: America's hyperscale bit barns draw as much power as entire states
item.description: Just 403 hyperscale datacenters consumed an estimated 1.8 percent of US electricity in 2024-25, and their carbon dioxide emissions were roughly two to three times an earlier forecast for 2018. Research led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative looked specifically at hyperscale facilities, the largest class of server farms that typically support cloud computing and AI processing. The published study, " Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres ," estimates their combined electricity use approached that of a single state such as Indiana, Michigan, or Tennessee under the highest-load scenario. The researchers identified 403 hyperscale facilities by using a larger datacenter dataset, satellite imagery, and building footprints on OpenStreetMap. Rather than reading electricity meters, the researchers worked out consumption from each site's electrical capacity, the hours in a year, and assumptions about how heavily the facility was running. Across four operating scenarios, ranging from low-intensity use to AI-heavy workloads, electricity draw was believed to total 68-99 terawatt-hours (TWh). Each of those states consumed approximately 100 TWh during the study period. The researchers also calculated carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions using eGRID2023 plant-level generation and emissions data from the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Emissions ranged from 21 million to 31 million metric tons of CO 2 across the scenarios, with a central estimate of 25.7 million. That compares with 10.5 million for 2018. The study covered May 2024 to April 2025, so electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely to be even higher now, the researchers say. "What we're seeing is already striking, but it's only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry," said Gianluca Guidi, lead author on the paper and postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard. "The datacenter boom hasn't slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we're reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026." Harvard's report also considers the mix of fuels being used to generate the electricity that powers all those hyperscale data houses. The mix varies considerably between regional grids, so where a hyperscale facility is built makes a substantial difference to its attributed emissions. Across the sites studied, roughly 54 percent of the electricity attributed to their consumption came from fossil fuels, mainly natural gas and coal. The electricity attributed to these facilities nevertheless had a lower average carbon intensity than the US grid overall. item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 17, 1967: NASA's Surveyor 6 moon probe makes 1st-ever successful launch and hop from the lunar surface
item.description: null On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface. Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the big liftoff. First Surveyor 6 launched from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off. Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11 . A panorama of the moon from NASA's Surveyor 6 moon lander in November 1967. (Image credit: NASA/GSFC/LROC) Why it mattered NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft launched to the moon on Nov. 7, 1967 and made its first landing on the lunar surface on Nov. 10 of that year. It's primary mission was to make a soft landing on the moon in the Sinus Medii of the moon. The probe took nearly 30,000 photos of the moon during its 16 days on the lunar surface, with the lander shutting down due to the onset of lunar night on Nov. 26. Surveyor 6 was the sixth and penultimate moon mission of NASA's Surveyor lunar program, so a lot of what it did (launching and landing on the moon ) had been done before. But a lunar liftoff? That was something new. This Boeing diagram depicts the short launch and hop on the moon by NASA's Surveyor 6 moon lander on Nov. 17, 1967. (Image credit: NASA/GSFC/LROC via Boeing) "On November 17, as an engineering test to see if its rockets could be restarted on the Moon, Surveyor’s engines fired for 2.5 seconds, lifting the spacecraft 12 feet high and moving it 8 feet west of its original landing site, in the first powered liftoff from another celestial body," NASA wrote in a mission overview . The engineering test proved that a spacecraft could land on the moon, and then lift off and take flight once more. That capability was a core requirement for NASA's Apollo astronaut moon landings that followed, since astronauts needed a way to return home after visiting the moon. But there was critical science Surveyor 6 was able to do with the lunar hop. "This maneuver provided excellent views of the surface disturbances produced by the initial landing and the effects of firing rocket engines close to the lunar surface," scientists with the Lunar and Planetary Institute wrote in a summary . "Photography obtained after the hop contributed to the soil mechanics investigation." Surveyor 6 also had a bar magnet on its footpad that allowed scientists to test how magnetic the lunar regolith was at the landing site. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: NICER Status Updates
item.description: November 17, 2026 NASA’s NICER Telescope Ends Science Operations After studying the universe for six and a half years beyond its initial mission, NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer) telescope on the International Space Station has ended science operations. The mission and space station teams are now focused on plans to finalize NICER’s 8-year archive of X-ray science observations and decommission and detach the telescope from its perch near the station’s starboard solar array. In June 2025, NICER was suddenly unable to swivel side-to-side beyond its current orientation, which limited its ability to track cosmic objects. The team paused data collection to investigate the issue. Robotic cameras on the outside of the station collected photographs of NICER that helped eliminate external causes. After an extensive investigation, engineers think an internal motor has failed, limiting the telescope’s motion. Launched in 2017, NICER embarked on an initial 18-month prime mission. Since then, it has made groundbreaking measurements of neutron stars , which contain the densest matter in the universe that we can measure, and revolutionized our understanding of black holes , active galaxies , and other mysterious phenomena in our universe. The telescope also successfully demonstrated the potential of pulsar-based spacecraft navigation in X-rays that could be used for travel to Mars and beyond. Closer to home, technology developed to test NICER before launch is being incorporated into prototype portable CT scanners , materials analysis systems, and other applications. August 5, 2025 Science Observations Remain Paused for NASA’s NICER Telescope Science operations by NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer), an X-ray telescope on the International Space Station, remain paused as the team continues to evaluate the telescope’s systems after an issue developed with one of its motors. The motor is unable to move NICER beyond its current position side to side, and the telescope’s status has not changed since operations were halted June 17. The primary goal is to move NICER into its stowed configuration in case it needs to accommodate space station activities, though the current placement does not pose a safety issue to the station or crew. The team currently does not have a timeframe for returning to science operations. Photos taken by robotic cameras outside the station are helping eliminate external causes for the issue. Now the team is coordinating with space station personnel to perform troubleshooting maneuvers and determine potential causes within the payload. Since it began observing the X-ray universe in 2017, NICER has successfully demonstrated a form of deep space navigation that could be used for travel to Mars and beyond. item.title: Situational Awareness Dumps Bitcoin Miners After Citadel Sale
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Situational Awareness Dumps Bitcoin Miners After Citadel Sale Situational Awareness, the artificial intelligence hedge fund run by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, cut its bitcoin miner holdings sharply in the third quarter, leaving about $80.8 million across three stocks and exiting three others, a Monday filing shows. The San Francisco firm still held 3,019,029 CleanSpark shares, worth $38.9 million at Sept. 30, 1,934,618 Bitdeer shares, worth $20.3 million, and 527,864 IREN shares, worth $21.6 million. Those are the only miner lines left, a sliver of the $1.83 billion in six miner stocks the fund listed at June 30. IREN Cut 94%, and three miners are gone The deepest cut was IREN. The fund held 9,474,099 IREN shares, worth $433.3 million, at midyear. The Sept. 30 stake is about 94% smaller by share count. CleanSpark was trimmed about 75%, from 12,276,139 shares worth $178.6 million. Bitdeer was reduced about 44%, from 3,439,450 shares worth $54.6 million. Bitdeer’s reported value fell further than its share count, to $20.3 million, as the stock also declined. Three names disappeared from the filing entirely. The fund had held 26,008,473 Core Scientific shares, worth $665.6 million, 17,100,000 Riot Platforms shares, worth $468.2 million, and 9,133,726 Hive Digital shares, worth $33.2 million, at June 30. None of those lines appear in the new report. The filing does not say whether those sales were part of a late-July portfolio sale, later trades, or both. An AI thesis that ran through Bitcoin miners Aschenbrenner published a long 2024 essay, “Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead,” arguing that artificial general intelligence was approaching faster than most investors appreciated, and that computing power and electricity would be the tight constraints. He founded the fund that September around that view, looking at technology and energy companies that AI would help or hurt. The miner stakes fit the same idea. A March profile described the fund as betting that electricity and computing capacity may be the most valuable assets in the AI build-out, pointing to miners that were turning high-density facilities and power contracts toward AI workloads. IREN has signed a multiyear cloud contract with Microsoft. CleanSpark has struck a $6.6 billion data-center lease. Listed miners have also been operating under tight economics this year, with bitcoin often trading below estimated production costs. A July sale to Citadel, then a much smaller filing The cuts landed after a brutal July. The fund sold the bulk of the fund’s public stock portfolio to Ken Griffin’s Citadel late that month after heavy losses on AI-related holdings, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Those sources said the fund was forced to unwind most of its public book. In a letter to investors, Aschenbrenner said the portfolio was down an estimated 67% in July, that the fund had come “closer to permanent capital impairment than is acce

The July 2026 hack of Hugging Face and other attacks carried out by OpenAI's autonomous agents "may just be the tip of the iceberg," said a lawsuit filed in a state court by California Attorney General Rob Bonta. "OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General’s Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing." OpenAI had publicly reported only 27 such incidents, showing that "OpenAI’s public reports do not represent the full scope of loss-of-control incidents involving OpenAI’s models that have impacted third parties," the lawsuit said. OpenAI "knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it," Bonta said in a press release . Read full article Comments

item.title: Inspiring FOSS project Crosspoint Reader has lessons about tech, communities, and LLMs
item.description: The Ubuntu Summit isn't all about Ubuntu, or even Linux. The second day opened with a talk from CrossPoint Reader project lead Justin Mitchell, with both good and bad news for all kinds of FOSS. The talk, EPUBs, ESP32s, and Everyone's A Developer Now , was all about a FOSS project that isn't Linux-based – because the devices it targets are much too small to run even the smallest, most cut-down distro. Recently, a new generation of roughly credit-card sized ebook readers has been thriving. Some have integral magnets, which let them cling to the back of iPhones – or to models with magnetically attached wireless chargers, anyway. The idea is that instead of waking your phone and doom-scrolling, you flip it over and read a book. They are bringing about what Mitchell calls "the Tiktok-ification of reading." Many of them, though, come from their various manufacturers significantly limited by their original OSes. The strong sales are linked to the availability of free, open-source, cross-platform alternative firmware, which removes many of the restrictions that the devices ship with. For most of them, that means Crosspoint Reader . Some devices are now shipping, new, with versions of Crosspoint Reader. This runs on multiple different models of compact e-readers, and this small community project has seen impressively widespread adoption: over 300,000 installations. Early in his talk, project lead Mitchell mentioned more than 1,600 forks on GitHub, but at the time of writing, that's up to 2,300 and counting. He estimates nearly half a million users. This kind of success forced Crosspoint Reader to change from being FOSS code to a product. A peripheral example is the Brick Club List , a list of what versions work with what devices – an Excel spreadsheet that grew into a website. If you haven't been paying attention, you may not have noticed just how much e-readers have shrunk – in size and in cost – in the last few years. The Reg FOSS desk first noticed this trend in 2024, when we read about the smartphone-sized Onyx Palma , which sold for around $300 (about £225). As it happens, this was a decade after The Register first looked at one of Boox's devices . Mini e-readers – and their prices – have continued shrinking since. The $99 (£75) Xteink X4 Classic has a 4.- inch (10.9 cm) screen, and the $79 (£59) Xteink X3 is even smaller: it's the size of a credit card, with a 3.7-inch (9.4 cm) screen. As a result of their strong sales, there are now multiple similar devices on sale, such as the Boox Picco . The project's GitHub page lists 11 devices it currently supports, all of which are based around the ESP32-C3 system on a chip. The ESP32-C series chips are more powerful than the earlier models of ESP32 microcontrollers: they have a single RISC-V core, but running in the low hundreds of MHz and with some 400 kB of RAM, of which about 380 kB is available. It's very little space, but enough to have fun. Mitchell talked about some of the problems of being a FOSS p

item.title: Visa Report Identifies Opportunity to Integrate Digital Payments with SMEs Business Operations in Nigeria
item.description: Report identifies next SME digitization opportunity: connecting payments with day-to-day business management. 94% of SMEs surveyed find an all-in-one payment and business solution appealing, yet only 29% currently use one, pointing to untapped demand for tools that connect payments with business management. Integrated payment and business solutions can give financial institutions a more holistic view of SME cash flow and support more tailored financing solutions over time. Small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Nigeria have largely moved beyond the first stage of digital payment adoption, but a productivity gap remains. According to Visa’s new survey for its Pay and Get Paid 2026 report, most of the SMEs surveyed in Nigeria use digital payments, showing how firmly digital commerce has taken root in the country’s small business economy. However, many SMEs still manage the related financial and operational tasks separately, with only 29% currently using an integrated solution that connects payments with broader business management. The report shows that financial admin and disconnected tools create friction for SMEs, with surveyed businesses citing challenges in tracking outstanding invoices (14%), keeping payroll records organized (19%), and preparing financial reports (16%). These pain points reflect a disconnect between payments and the operational tasks that follow, with some businesses juggling multiple systems to keep their business running. The appetite for a more connected approach is clear. According to the report, 94% of SMEs find an all-in-one payment and business solution appealing, reflecting strong interest in tools that can bring payments and key business operations into one experience. However, adoption has yet to catch up: only 29% of SMEs currently use an integrated payment and business platform. The report points to several perception barriers that may be slowing adoption. Businesses cited that they already have manual processes that work (8%), that an integrated platform may disrupt their current way of working (8%), or that they do not trust relying on a single provider (7%). These findings suggest that broader adoption will depend on helping SMEs better understand how integrated tools can be relevant, accessible, and scalable for businesses at different stages of growth. At the same time, the experience of SMEs already using integrated solutions suggests a strong value case. The report found that Nigerian businesses using an integrated tool or platform report 93% satisfaction, with 88% reporting efficiency gains, including reductions in the time and effort required to manage their business. Beyond efficiency, integrated platforms may also create new opportunities for financial institutions to deepen SME relationships by using richer payments and business-management data to better understand cash flow patterns, support risk assessment, and potentially enable more relevant lending solutions over time. Andrew Uaboi , Vice

item.title: SAP's cloud migration chief is migrating to Ionos as CEO
item.description: SAP chief customer officer Thomas Saueressig is leaving the German software giant to become CEO of hosting and cloud provider Ionos. The ERP and biz application vendor confirmed his departure on Tuesday, saying he will remain responsible for his current duties until the end of March 2027. He will succeed Ionos CEO Achim Weiß on April 1. In January, Saueressig will begin handing over responsibilities to Emmanuel Raptopoulos, currently a regional customer success president, who will take charge on an interim basis. SAP's supervisory board is searching for a permanent successor. Saueressig joined SAP's executive board in 2019 and became chief customer officer in April 2026. He leads the Customer Value Group and is charged with overseeing sales, customer success, services, and delivery, including adoption of SAP's cloud and AI products. In previous roles at SAP, Saueressig was responsible for customer services and delivery. He has also led product engineering, and has served as SAP's in-house CIO responsible for IT strategy and cloud transformation. He joined SAP in 2004 through its combined work-and-study program. His departure follows several changes at the top of SAP in recent years. In September 2024, CTO Jürgen Müller left by mutual agreement following an "incident" at a company event earlier in the year. In a statement, Müller said his behavior had been inappropriate. The company announced he would get paid €7.1 million following his departure. Chief revenue officer Scott Russell also left in 2024 by mutual agreement with the supervisory board. Julia White left the role of chief marketing and solutions officer in August 2024. "Thomas Saueressig has been a valued member of the Executive Board and has made significant contributions to SAP's transformation," said Pekka Ala-Pietilä, chair of SAP's supervisory board. "Over many years, he has helped sharpen SAP's focus on execution, customer value and operational excellence. We thank him for his commitment and wish him all the best for the future." Saueressig's departure comes as SAP pushes to move the ERP systems underpinning thousands of customers' businesses into the cloud – an effort whose operations and infrastructure he helped oversee. ®

item.title: NASA to Conduct Low-Altitude Flights Over Texas Farmland
item.description: Editor’s Note: This article was originally published on Oct. 15, 2026, and has been updated to correct the location and update the duration of the flight deployment. A NASA Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Amarillo, Texas, from Thursday, Oct. 22, through Monday, Nov. 2. These flights will measure gaseous and particulate emissions from animal feeding operations. A photo of the Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft, which will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Amarillo, Texas, to measure emissions in October and November 2026. Dynamic Aviation Agricultural emissions represent an important and understudied part of Earth’s land and atmosphere systems. The FarmFlux mission will deploy more than a dozen sensors to measure ozone, methane, ammonia, particulates, and other pollutants rising from crop lands and livestock farms and their interaction with the Earth’s atmosphere. The mission is jointly led by NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland; Colorado State University; and Boston University. Additional low-altitude research flights with a NASA P-3 Orion aircraft are scheduled for the March to July 2027 growing season in the Midwest and California’s Central Valley with a focus on cropland. For more information about the FarmFlux mission, visit: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/evs-4/farm-flux/ By Sharon Teitelbaum NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley

item.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5072-5076: The Return of the Polygons
item.description: Curiosity Navigation Curiosity Home Mission Overview Where is Curiosity? Mission Updates Science Overview Instruments Highlights Exploration Goals News and Features Multimedia Curiosity Raw Images Images Videos Audio Mosaics More Resources Mars Missions Mars Perseverance Rover Mars Curiosity Rover Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Mars Odyssey More Mars Missions Mars Home 2 min read Curiosity Blog, Sols 5072-5076: The Return of the Polygons NASA’s Mars rover Curiosity acquired this image of a portion of the area in front of the rover, in which the return of the regular, well-expressed polygons captured several weeks ago can be seen. Curiosity used its Mast Camera (MastCam) to capture this image on Sol 5073, or Martian day 5,073 of the Mars Science Laboratory mission, at 15:45:05 UTC. NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS Written by Abigail Fraeman, Deputy Project Scientist, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology Earth planning date: Friday, Nov. 13, 2026 Curiosity’s past several weeks have been very focused on drilling and analysis of the “Basque Lakes” and “Nazca” samples. We learned a lot from those drilled samples, but it’s time to hit the Martian road again and resume our climb up Mount Sharp. The Yardang unit on the upper part of the mountain is calling! As we climb higher on Mount Sharp, we’ll continue to use many of our less resource intensive science instruments like APXS, ChemCam, MAHLI, and Mastcam to document the chemistry and textures of the rocks we encounter while making purposeful upward progress. These measurements allow us to document changes in the environments that formed the rocks and that altered them over time. The two areas we explored this week had rocks that were crisscrossed by lots of small, regular sized polygons surrounded by raised ridges. This texture was very similar to the rocks we encountered a few months ago slightly lower on the mountain . Those unique textures really surprised us when we first saw them, and we’ve been spending time as a science team discussing how they may have formed. Polygonal textures like these can form under a variety of different conditions including shrinkage of the surface when water is lost from minerals, temperature cycling, or compaction and expansion after being buried and exposed. The data Curiosity collected this week give us more clues about the genesis of these features and what they reveal about the evolution of Mars’ habitability. We’ll also get information about the composition of the cements that form the raised ridges around the polygons. In the orbital view of our future route, I can see the layers that we’ll reach next week or the week after have textures very similar to where we first saw the amazing field of polygons. So I’m guessing we’ll continue to encounter polygons in the next couple drives, and that they’ll look more dramatic and expansive with each drive. But this is just a guess! item.title: Opting out of Gemini tracking? Google will still hold your data 20x longer
item.description: Opting out of Gemini chat retention is about to mean a lot less thanks to a quietly announced Google update. Google on Monday said that it was making changes to Gemini chat history that, at first glance, makes it seem like users are simply getting more control over their discussions with the Chocolate Factory’s chatbot. At the core of the announcement is Google's splitting of Gemini chat history settings from AI model training permissions. What that means is that users will now be able to store their chat histories with Gemini without also having to opt in to allow their conversations to be used to train those same models, as was previously the case. So far so good: Being able to have Gemini remember more of your past interactions to contextualize newer discussions is nice, to be sure. The second part of the announcement, however, might raise one's privacy hackles. "Now, if you turn your new History setting off, future chats will be saved for around two months," Google notes. "They're used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public." Google said it is making that change in the name of making Gemini safer and more secure, but it fails to mention that the chat retention period for users who turned their history off had been just 72 hours before this update. That's right: Prior to Monday's change, Gemini users who turned off the "Keep Activity" option only had their chats retained for three days, according to an archived copy of the same page that now states that choosing the same please-don't-store-my-AI-chats option means Google keeps them "for around two months." It's also worth noting that, even if users have the option to not store Gemini chat records enabled, submitting a feedback request on any Gemini post means that temporary retention period gets extended to three years. That was the case both before and after Monday's change, mind you, but for the privacy-conscious it's definitely important to note. Sending feedback to Google about a Gemini response also means that humans will be reviewing that particular conversation, as well as any associated files and conversations that can be associated with the one in question. Submitting feedback also means that Google assumes the right to use the conversation and its associated content to improve its services and improve its AI models. In other words, even if you opt out of having your conversations stored, your Gemini history could still end up being used to feed the Google machine. The company didn't respond to questions for this story. ®

item.title: NASA wants you to 'shine bright' today for Voyager 1's light-day milestone. Here's how
item.description: null As NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft prepares to reach a historic distance from Earth, the agency is inviting people around the world to celebrate by shining a light into the night sky in honor of humanity's farthest-flung spacecraft. The event, called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," will take place after sunset on Tuesday (Nov. 17), the day before Voyager 1 gets one light-day from Earth . And that's a big milestone: One light-day is the distance light travels in a day — about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers). NASA is encouraging "Shine Bright" participants to create a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet by flashing the spacecraft's three-letter mission call sign, VGR, in Morse code, according to a statement from the space agency. To celebrate the spacecraft, participants can use a flashlight, phone, bike light or other portable light source to send the signal skyward. And don't fret if you're unfamiliar with Morse code : NASA has created an automated flasher that can be opened in a smartphone or tablet browser to display the VGR sequence. The spacecraft’s call sign pattern consists of three quick flashes followed by one long flash for the letter V, two long flashes and one quick flash for G, and one quick flash, one long flash and another quick flash for R. Participants are encouraged to repeat the sequence for about a minute, NASA officials said. The three-letter call sign for NASA's Voyager mission, VGR, spelled out in Morse code. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) NASA also invites people to photograph or record their light signals and share them on social media, tagging the agency's official account, @NASA. The goal is to create a worldwide display of light marking a milestone nearly five decades in the making. The celebration is intended as a symbolic tribute rather than an actual attempt to communicate with Voyager 1 . At a distance of one light-day from Earth, the spacecraft is so far away that even radio signals traveling at the speed of light take approximately 24 hours to reach it. A flashlight or phone signal from Earth, of course, cannot reach the probe; NASA communicates with it using its Deep Space Network of radio dishes. Voyager 1 will get one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Launched on Sept. 5, 1977, Voyager 1 has spent nearly 50 years traveling through space and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth. When it reaches the one-light-day milestone, it will have traveled a distance that light itself takes 24 hours to cross. Its twin, Voyager 2 , is expected to reach the same milestone in November 2035. (The two spacecraft took different routes through the solar system.) The public celebration will be followed by another opportunity to learn more about the historic mission.
